casadi::Sparsity Class Reference

#include <sparsity.hpp>

Detailed Description

The storage format is a compressed column storage (CCS) format.
In this format, the structural non-zero elements are stored in column-major order, starting from the upper left corner of the matrix and ending in the lower right corner.

In addition to the dimension (size1(), size2()), (i.e. the number of rows and the number of columns respectively), there are also two vectors of integers:

  1. "colind" [length size2()+1], which contains the index to the first non-zero element on or after the corresponding column. All the non-zero elements of a particular column i are thus the elements with index el that fulfills: colind[i] <= el < colind[i+1].
  2. "row" [same length as the number of non-zero elements, nnz()] The rows for each of the structural non-zeros.

Note that with this format, it is cheap to loop over all the non-zero elements of a particular column, at constant time per element, but expensive to jump to access a location (i, j).

If the matrix is dense, i.e. length(row) == size1()*size2(), the format reduces to standard dense column major format, which allows access to an arbitrary element in constant time.

Since the object is reference counted (it inherits from SharedObject), several matrices are allowed to share the same sparsity pattern.

The implementations of methods marked as such in this class has been taken from the CSparse package and modified to fit CasADi data structures and separation of sparsity pattern calculation and numerical evaluation. These functions are Copyright(c) Timothy A. Davis, 2006-2009 and licensed as a derivative work under the GNU LGPL

Every DM, SX and MX carries a pattern, obtained with sparsity(), and a symbolic or numeric matrix can be created from one, e.g. SX.sym("x", sp) or DM(sp, 1). Entries outside the pattern are structural zeros: they are never stored and never computed with. The row indices within a column are strictly increasing.

Patterns are immutable and cached: constructing a pattern that already exists returns a reference to the cached object, so equal patterns are cheap to compare. The in-place methods (resize, enlarge, erase, append, add_nz, ...) rebind the object to a new pattern rather than modify the shared one. Use is_equal or the == operator to compare patterns; object identity is not meaningful in the target languages.

A default-constructed Sparsity is a null object (is_null() is true): it carries no pattern and most methods raise an error on it. It is used as "no pattern" sentinel, e.g. as the result of a coloring that exceeds its cutoff. Empty patterns are allowed: a 0-by-n or n-by-0 pattern has no nonzeros, is dense, and is_empty() is true for it.

   >>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
   >>> DM(sp, 1)
   DM(
   [[1, 00, 00, 1],
    [00, 00, 1, 00],
    [1, 00, 00, 00]])
   >>> sp
   Sparsity(3x4,4nz)
   >>> sp.size1(), sp.size2(), sp.nnz(), sp.numel()
   (3, 4, 4, 12)
   >>> sp.colind(), sp.row()
   ([0, 2, 2, 3, 4], [0, 2, 1, 0])
   >>> sp == Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
   True
   >>> SX.sym("x", sp)
   SX(
   [[x_0, 00, 00, x_3],
    [00, 00, x_2, 00],
    [x_1, 00, 00, 00]])
   >>> Sparsity.dense(0, 3), Sparsity().is_null()
   (Sparsity(0x3), True)

   >> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
   >> DM(sp, 1)
   [[1, 00, 00, 1],
    [00, 00, 1, 00],
    [1, 00, 00, 00]]
   >> sp
   3x4,4nz
   >> fprintf('%d %d %d %d\n', sp.size1(), sp.size2(), sp.nnz(), sp.numel())
   3 4 4 12
   >> sp.colind(), sp.row()
   0 2 2 3 4
   0 2 1 0
   >> sp == Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
   1
   >> SX.sym('x', sp)
   [[x_0, 00, 00, x_3],
    [00, 00, x_2, 00],
    [x_1, 00, 00, 00]]
   >> Sparsity.dense(0, 3), Sparsity().is_null()
   0x3
   1

   julia> sp = ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
   julia> ca.DM(sp, 1)
   DM(
   [[1, 00, 00, 1],
    [00, 00, 1, 00],
    [1, 00, 00, 00]])
   julia> sp
   Sparsity(3x4,4nz)
   julia> ca.size1(sp), ca.size2(sp), ca.nnz(sp), ca.numel(sp)
   (3, 4, 4, 12)
   julia> ca.colind(sp), ca.row(sp)
   ([0, 2, 2, 3, 4], [0, 2, 1, 0])
   julia> ca.is_equal(sp, ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]))
   true
   julia> ca.SX.sym("x", sp)
   SX(
   [[x_0, 00, 00, x_3],
    [00, 00, x_2, 00],
    [x_1, 00, 00, 00]])
   julia> ca.Sparsity.dense(0, 3), ca.is_null(ca.Sparsity())
   (0x3, true)

◆ Sparsity() [1/5]

casadi::Sparsity::Sparsity ( casadi_int  dummy = 0)
explicit

is_null() is true for the result and most other methods raise an error on it. A null Sparsity is the "no pattern" sentinel used by e.g. uni_coloring (as default for AT) and returned by the colorings when the cutoff is exceeded.

Parameters
dummyMust be 0 (any other value raises an error)

>>> sp = Sparsity()
>>> sp.is_null(), sp
(True, Sparsity(NULL))
>>> try: sp.nnz()
... except Exception as e: print("error")
error


>> sp = Sparsity();
>> sp.is_null(), sp
1
NULL
>> try, sp.nnz(); catch e, disp('error'); end
error


julia> sp = ca.Sparsity();
julia> ca.is_null(sp), sp
(true, NULL)
julia> try
           ca.nnz(sp)
       catch e
           println("error")
       end
error

nrowNumber of rows
ncolNumber of columns
colindColumn offsets, length ncol+1, colind[0] == 0, nondecreasing
rowRow index of each nonzero, length colind[ncol], each in [0, nrow), strictly increasing within a column

◆ add_nz()

casadi_int casadi::Sparsity::add_nz ( casadi_int  rr,
casadi_int  cc 
)

Returns the position of the entry among the nonzeros. If the entry is a structural zero, the object is rebound to a pattern that includes it (nonzero indices after it shift by one). Negative indices count from the end. An index out of bounds raises an error.

>>> sp = Sparsity(3, 3)
>>> sp.add_nz(1, 1), sp.add_nz(0, 0), sp.add_nz(1, 1), sp
(0, 0, 1, Sparsity(3x3,2nz))
>>> DM(sp, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 00]])
>>> try: sp.add_nz(3, 0)
... except Exception as e: print("out of bounds")
out of bounds


>> sp = Sparsity(3, 3);
>> [sp.add_nz(1, 1), sp.add_nz(0, 0), sp.add_nz(1, 1)], sp
0 0 1
3x3,2nz
>> DM(sp, 1)
[[1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 00]]
>> try, sp.add_nz(3, 0); catch e, disp('out of bounds'); end
out of bounds


julia> sp = ca.Sparsity(3, 3);
julia> ca.add_nz(sp, 1, 1), ca.add_nz(sp, 0, 0), ca.add_nz(sp, 1, 1)
(0, 0, 1)
julia> ca.DM(sp, 1)

◆ amd()

std::vector< casadi_int > casadi::Sparsity::amd ( ) const

Fill-reducing ordering p to apply to a symmetric linear system before factorization: factorize A[p, p] instead of A. The pattern must be symmetric, otherwise an error is raised; for an unsymmetric A, order the pattern of A^T*A (as qr_sparse does). Used by ldl and qr_sparse when their amd argument is true.

The implementation is a modified version of cs_amd in CSparse Copyright(c) Timothy A. Davis, 2006-2009 Licensed as a derivative work under the GNU LGPL

>>> Sparsity.banded(4, 1).amd(), Sparsity.dense(3, 3).amd(), Sparsity(0, 0).amd()
([3, 2, 0, 1], [0, 1, 2], [])
>>> try: Sparsity.upper(3).amd()
... except Exception as e: print("not symmetric")
not symmetric


>> Sparsity.banded(4, 1).amd(), Sparsity.dense(3, 3).amd()

0 1 2
>> isempty(Sparsity(0, 0).amd())
1
>> try, Sparsity.upper(3).amd(); catch e, disp('not symmetric'); end

◆ btf()

casadi_int casadi::Sparsity::btf ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  rowperm,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  colperm,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  rowblock,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  colblock,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  coarse_rowblock,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  coarse_colblock 
) const

Computes a row permutation and a column permutation that bring the pattern into block upper triangular form, see Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems by Davis (2006). The pattern may be rectangular.

Returns
  • the number of fine blocks nb
  • rowperm, colperm: row and column permutation vectors, so that A[rowperm, colperm] is in block upper triangular form
  • rowblock, colblock (length nb+1): block k spans rows rowblock[k] to rowblock[k+1]-1 and columns colblock[k] to colblock[k+1]-1 of the permuted matrix
  • coarse_rowblock, coarse_colblock (length 5): boundaries of the coarse decomposition into the underdetermined, square (well-determined) and overdetermined parts; coarse_colblock[3] is the structural rank (sprank)

Only structure is used: the distance of entries to the diagonal plays no role, so a randomly permuted block-diagonal matrix is not necessarily brought back to block diagonal form, and the row and column permutations differ in general, which destroys symmetry. The result is cached in the pattern.

The implementation is a modified version of cs_dmperm in CSparse Copyright(c) Timothy A. Davis, 2006-2009 Licensed as a derivative work under the GNU LGPL

>>> B = Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 1, 2])
>>> DM(B, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00, 1],
 [00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 1]])
>>> nb, rowperm, colperm, rowblock, colblock, crb, ccb = B.btf()
>>> nb, rowperm, colperm, rowblock, colblock
(3, [2, 0, 1], [2, 0, 1], [0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 2, 3])
>>> crb, ccb
([0, 0, 0, 3, 3], [0, 0, 3, 3, 3])
>>> DM(B, 1)[rowperm, colperm]
DM(
[[1, 00, 00],
 [1, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 1]])
>>> sprank(Sparsity.nonzeros(3, 3, [0, 1, 2])), sprank(Sparsity.diag(3))
(1, 3)

◆ combine() [1/2]

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::combine ( const Sparsity &  y,
bool  f0x_is_zero,
bool  function0_is_zero 
) const

Models the pattern of f(x, y) applied elementwise, where y has this pattern's shape. An entry is kept in the result when both arguments are nonzero; an entry where only y is nonzero is kept unless f0x_is_zero (f(0, y) == 0) and an entry where only x is nonzero is kept unless function0_is_zero (f(x, 0) == 0). So combine(y, False, False) is the union (unite) and combine(y, True, True) is the intersection (intersect). A shape mismatch raises an error.

The C++ overload with mapping returns, per nonzero of the union, bit 1 if the first argument is nonzero, bit 2 if the second is and bit 4 if the entry was dropped from the result.

Parameters
yPattern with the same shape
f0x_is_zeroTrue if entries where only y is nonzero are structural zeros
function0_is_zeroTrue if entries where only this pattern is nonzero are structural zeros

>>> a = Sparsity.diag(2)
>>> b = Sparsity.triplet(2, 2, [0, 1], [1, 1])
>>> a.combine(b, False, False) == a + b, a.combine(b, True, True) == a * b
(True, True)
>>> DM(a.combine(b, True, False), 1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> DM(a.combine(b, False, True), 1)
DM(
[[00, 1],
 [00, 1]])


>> a = Sparsity.diag(2);
>> b = Sparsity.triplet(2, 2, [0, 1], [1, 1]);
>> a.combine(b, false, false) == a + b, a.combine(b, true, true) == a .* b
1
1
>> DM(a.combine(b, true, false), 1)
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]]
>> DM(a.combine(b, false, true), 1)
[[00, 1],
 [00, 1]]


julia> a = ca.Sparsity.diag(2);
julia> b = ca.Sparsity.triplet(2, 2, [0, 1], [1, 1]);
julia> ca.is_equal(ca.combine(a, b, false, false), ca.unite(a, b))
true
julia> ca.DM(ca.combine(a, b, true, false), 1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
julia> ca.DM(ca.combine(a, b, false, true), 1)
DM(
[[00, 1],
 [00, 1]])

unite, intersect

◆ compress()

std::vector< casadi_int > casadi::Sparsity::compress ( bool  canonical = true) const

Returns [nrow, ncol, colind..., row...], the layout accepted by compressed() and used for sparsity patterns in generated C code. With canonical false, a dense pattern is abbreviated to [nrow, ncol, 1] (an abbreviation that compressed() given a vector does not accept).

>>> Sparsity.diag(2).compress()
[2, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1]
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).compress()
[2, 2, 0, 2, 4, 0, 1, 0, 1]
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).compress(False)
[2, 2, 1]
>>> Sparsity(0, 2).compress()
[0, 2, 0, 0, 0]


>> Sparsity.diag(2).compress()
2 2 0 1 2 0 1
>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).compress()
2 2 0 2 4 0 1 0 1
>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).compress(false)
2 2 1
>> Sparsity(0, 2).compress()
0 2 0 0 0


julia> println(ca.compress(ca.Sparsity.diag(2)))
[2, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1]
julia> println(ca.compress(ca.Sparsity.dense(2, 2)))
[2, 2, 0, 2, 4, 0, 1, 0, 1]
julia> println(ca.compress(ca.Sparsity.dense(2, 2), false))
[2, 2, 1]
julia> println(ca.compress(ca.Sparsity(0, 2)))

◆ compressed() [1/2]

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::compressed ( const casadi_int *  v,
bool  order_rows = false 
)
static

The vector is laid out as [nrow, ncol, colind (ncol+1 entries), row (colind[ncol] entries)]. This is the format returned by compress() and used by generated C code (casadi_int arrays). When colind[ncol] equals nrow*ncol the row entries may be omitted (a dense pattern). An inconsistent vector raises an error.

Parameters
vCompact representation
order_rowsIf true, unsorted row indices within a column are sorted instead of raising an error

>>> sp = Sparsity.compressed([3, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 2])
>>> DM(sp, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> Sparsity.compressed(sp.compress()) == sp
True
>>> Sparsity.compressed([2, 2, 0, 2, 4])
Sparsity(2x2)


>> sp = Sparsity.compressed([3, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 2]);

[[1, 00],
 [00, 00],
 [00, 1]]
>> Sparsity.compressed(sp.compress()) == sp
1
>> Sparsity.compressed([2, 2, 0, 2, 4])
2x2

◆ dense() [1/2]

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::dense ( casadi_int  nrow,
casadi_int  ncol = 1 
)
static

All nrow*ncol entries are nonzeros, stored column by column. This is the pattern of every matrix created without an explicit sparsity, e.g. SX.sym("x", 2, 3).

Parameters
nrowNumber of rows, nonnegative
ncolNumber of columns, nonnegative; default 1 (a dense column vector)

The shape can also be given as a single pair (nrow, ncol).

>>> sp = Sparsity.dense(2, 3)
>>> sp, sp.nnz(), sp.is_dense()
(Sparsity(2x3), 6, True)
>>> sp.colind(), sp.row()
([0, 2, 4, 6], [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])
>>> Sparsity.dense(3), Sparsity.dense((2, 3))
(Sparsity(3x1), Sparsity(2x3))
>>> Sparsity.dense(0, 3).nnz(), Sparsity.dense(0, 3).is_dense()
(0, True)

inlinestatic

All nrow*ncol entries are nonzeros, stored column by column. This is the pattern of every matrix created without an explicit sparsity, e.g. SX.sym("x", 2, 3).

◆ dfs()

casadi_int casadi::Sparsity::dfs ( casadi_int  j,
casadi_int  top,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  SWIG_INOUT1xi,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  SWIG_INOUT2pstack,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  pinv,
std::vector< bool > &  SWIG_INOUT3marked 
) const

Low-level building block of scc (cs_dfs in CSparse). Starting from column j, it visits the columns reachable through the nonzeros and writes them, in reverse finishing order, into xi below position top. See Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems by Davis (2006).

Parameters
jStart node (column)
topCurrent top of the output stack in xi
xiOutput stack, length at least size2(); the visited nodes are stored in xi[new_top:top]
pstackWork vector, length at least size2()
pinvInverse row permutation, or an empty vector for none
markedVisited flags per node, updated in place
Returns
The new top of the stack, with the updated xi, pstack and marked vectors

>>> Sparsity.banded(3, 1).dfs(0, 3, [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [], [False] * 3)
(0, [0, 1, 2], [1, 4, 5], [True, True, True])


>> sp = Sparsity.banded(3, 1); xi = [0, 0, 0]; pstack = [0, 0, 0];
>> [top, xi, pstack, marked] = sp.dfs(0, 3, xi, pstack, [], [false, false, false]);
>> top, xi, pstack, marked
0
0 1 2
1 4 5
1 1 1

◆ enlarge()

void casadi::Sparsity::enlarge ( casadi_int  nrow,
casadi_int  ncol,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  rr,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  cc,
bool  ind1 = false 
)

The existing nonzeros are kept and scattered: row i of the old pattern becomes row rr[i] and column j becomes column cc[j] of the new nrow-by-ncol pattern, so that B[rr, cc] has the old pattern. The new rows and columns are structural zeros. Nonzero indices are unchanged. The object is rebound to the new pattern.

Parameters
nrowNew number of rows
ncolNew number of columns
rrNew row of every old row: length size1(), strictly increasing, entries in [0, nrow); negative entries count from the end
ccNew column of every old column: length size2(), strictly increasing, entries in [0, ncol)
ind1If true, indices are one-based

A wrong length or an index out of range raises an error.

>>> sp = Sparsity.dense(2, 2)
>>> sp.enlarge(4, 3, [0, 3], [1, 2])
>>> DM(sp, 1)
DM(
[[00, 1, 1],

 [00, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 1]])

std::vector< casadi_int > casadi::Sparsity::erase ( const std::vector< casadi_int > &  rr,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  cc,
bool  ind1 = false 
)

The shape is unchanged: only the nonzeros in the block rr x cc are removed. An entry is removed when its row is in rr and its column is in cc, so an empty rr or cc removes nothing. Indices may be unsorted and negative (counting from the end); out of range raises an error. The object is rebound to the new pattern.

Parameters
rrRows of the block to clear
ccColumns of the block to clear
ind1If true, indices are one-based
Returns
Mapping of length nnz() of the result: nonzero k of the result was nonzero mapping[k] of the original pattern

>>> sp = Sparsity.dense(3, 3)
>>> mapping = sp.erase([0, 2], [1])
>>> DM(sp, 1), mapping

◆ etree()

std::vector< casadi_int > casadi::Sparsity::etree ( bool  ata = false) const

Returns, for every column, the index of its parent in the elimination tree, or -1 for a root. See Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems by Davis (2006). With ata false the result matches MATLAB's etree(A) with zero-based indices (the pattern is treated as symmetric, only the upper triangular part is used); with ata true it matches etree(A, 'col'), the tree of A'*A.

The implementation is a modified version of cs_etree in CSparse Copyright(c) Timothy A. Davis, 2006-2009 Licensed as a derivative work under the GNU LGPL

>>> Sparsity.banded(4, 1).etree(), Sparsity.diag(4).etree()
([1, 2, 3, -1], [-1, -1, -1, -1])
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 3).etree(True)
[1, 2, -1]


>> Sparsity.banded(4, 1).etree(), Sparsity.diag(4).etree()
1 2 3 -1
-1 -1 -1 -1
>> Sparsity.dense(2, 3).etree(true)
1 2 -1


julia> ca.etree(ca.Sparsity.banded(4, 1)), ca.etree(ca.Sparsity.diag(4))
([1, 2, 3, -1], [-1, -1, -1, -1])
julia> println(ca.etree(ca.Sparsity.dense(2, 3), true))
[1, 2, -1]

void casadi::Sparsity::export_code ( const std::string &  lang,

Only "matlab" is supported: the code defines the dimensions, one-based column and row indices and the nonzero values of a sparse matrix. The code is written to the standard output or to the given stream.

Parameters
langTarget language, must be "matlab"
optionsDictionary with
  • "name": name of the generated variable (default "sp")
  • "as_matrix": also emit "<name> = sparse(...)" (default true)
  • "nonzeros": list of strings used as the nonzero values (default: ones)
  • "indent_level": number of two-space indents (default 0)
  • "inline": not supported, true raises an error

An unknown option raises an error.

>>> Sparsity.diag(2, 3).export_code("matlab")
sp_m = 2;
sp_n = 3;
sp_j = [1, 2];
sp_i = [1, 2];
sp_v = ones(size(sp_i));

A_m = 2;
A_n = 2;
A_j = [1, 2];
A_i = [1, 2];

◆ find() [1/2]

std::vector< casadi_int > casadi::Sparsity::find ( bool  ind1 = SWIG_IND1) const

Returns, in nonzero order, the position each nonzero would have in a dense column-major matrix of the same shape: row + col*size1(). Indexing a dense matrix A of this shape with the result picks the entries that are nonzeros of the pattern. Inverse of nonzeros(). For a dense pattern this is 0, ..., numel()-1.

Parameters
ind1If true, the indices are one-based

>>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
>>> sp.find(), sp.find(True)
([0, 2, 7, 9], [1, 3, 8, 10])
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).find(), Sparsity(2, 2).find(), Sparsity(0, 3).find()
([0, 1, 2, 3], [], [])


>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
>> sp.find(), sp.find(false)
1 3 8 10
0 2 7 9
>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).find()
1 2 3 4
>> [isempty(Sparsity(2, 2).find()), isempty(Sparsity(0, 3).find())]
1 1


julia> sp = ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);

julia> println(ca.find(ca.Sparsity.dense(2, 2)))

◆ get_diag()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::get_diag ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  mapping) const

If the pattern is not a vector, the result is the min(nrow, ncol)-by-1 pattern of the main diagonal: it has a nonzero for every diagonal entry (i, i) present in the pattern. If the pattern is a row or column vector of length n, the result is the n-by-n pattern with the vector entries on the diagonal.

Returns
The pattern and a mapping: mapping[k] is the nonzero index in the original pattern of nonzero k of the result

>>> sp, mapping = Sparsity.banded(3, 1).get_diag()
>>> sp, mapping
(Sparsity(3x1), [0, 3, 6])
>>> sp, mapping = Sparsity.unit(3, 1).get_diag()
>>> DM(sp, 1), mapping
(DM(
[[00, 00, 00],

◆ get_nz() [1/3]

casadi_int casadi::Sparsity::get_nz ( casadi_int  rr,
casadi_int  cc 
) const

Negative indices count from the end. An index out of bounds raises an error. For a dense pattern the result is rr + cc*size1(). The returned index addresses the nonzeros() vector of a matrix with this pattern.

>>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
>>> sp.get_nz(0, 0), sp.get_nz(2, 0), sp.get_nz(1, 0), sp.get_nz(-1, 0)
(0, 1, -1, 1)
>>> try: sp.get_nz(3, 0)
... except Exception as e: print("out of bounds")
out of bounds


>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
>> [sp.get_nz(0, 0), sp.get_nz(2, 0), sp.get_nz(1, 0), sp.get_nz(-1, 0)]
0 1 -1 1
>> try, sp.get_nz(3, 0); catch e, disp('out of bounds'); end
out of bounds


julia> sp = ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
julia> ca.get_nz(sp, 0, 0), ca.get_nz(sp, 2, 0), ca.get_nz(sp, 1, 0), ca.get_nz(sp, -1, 0)
(0, 1, -1, 1)
julia> try
           ca.get_nz(sp, 3, 0)

out of bounds

Returns one index per (row, column) combination, in column-major order over the block (all rows of the first column first); -1 marks a structural zero. Indices must be in range (no negative indices); otherwise an error is raised.

◆ get_nz() [3/3]

void casadi::Sparsity::get_nz ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  indices) const

Each entry of indices is replaced by the nonzero index of that element, or by -1 if the element is a structural zero. Entries that are already negative are left alone. The indices need not be sorted. An index of numel() or more raises an error.

>>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3])
>>> sp.get_nz([0, 2, 4, 9, 1])
[0, 1, -1, 3, -1]
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).get_nz([3, 0])
[3, 0]


>> sp = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
>> sp.get_nz([0, 2, 4, 9, 1])
0 1 -1 3 -1
>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2).get_nz([3, 0])
3 0


julia> sp = ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 2, 3]);
julia> ca.get_nz(sp, [0, 2, 4, 9, 1])
5-element Vector{Int64}:
  0
  1
 -1
  3
 -1
julia> ca.get_nz(ca.Sparsity.dense(2, 2), [3, 0])
2-element Vector{Int64}:
 3
 0

◆ is_compactible()

bool casadi::Sparsity::is_compactible ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  row,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  col 
) const

If true, returns the (sorted) row and column index sets such that nz(i, j) <-> i in row and j in col. The nonzero buffer of a compactible matrix in CCS is laid out exactly as a column-major dense row.size() x col.size() matrix, so it can be consumed by dense kernels without gather/scatter. The index sets are returned in either case (the nonempty rows and columns); a pattern without nonzeros is compactible.

>>> ok, row, col = Sparsity.rowcol([0, 2], [0, 2], 3, 3).is_compactible()
>>> ok, row, col
(True, [0, 2], [0, 2])
>>> ok, row, col = Sparsity.diag(3).is_compactible()
>>> ok, row, col
(False, [0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])


>> [ok, row, col] = Sparsity.rowcol([0, 2], [0, 2], 3, 3).is_compactible();
>> ok, row, col
1
0 2
0 2
>> [ok, row, col] = Sparsity.diag(3).is_compactible(); disp(ok), disp(row), disp(col)
0
0 1 2
0 1 2


julia> ca.is_compactible(ca.Sparsity.rowcol([0, 2], [0, 2], 3, 3))
(true, [0, 2], [0, 2])
julia> ca.is_compactible(ca.Sparsity.diag(3))
(false, [0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])

◆ is_equal() [1/3]

True when the dimensions and the nonzero positions coincide. This is the comparison behind the == operator. Shared (cached) patterns are detected in constant time; otherwise colind and row are compared. The second overload compares against a pattern given in compressed column storage vectors.

True
>>> Sparsity.dense(2, 2) == Sparsity.dense(2, 3)
False
>>> Sparsity(2, 2) == Sparsity.dense(2, 2)
False


>> a = Sparsity.diag(2);

>> Sparsity(2, 2) == Sparsity.dense(2, 2)
0

◆ is_orthonormal()

bool casadi::Sparsity::is_orthonormal ( bool  allow_empty = false) const

Without allow_empty the pattern must also be square with exactly one nonzero per row and column (a permutation pattern). With allow_empty, rows and columns without nonzeros are disregarded and the shape may be rectangular.

Parameters
allow_emptyDisregard empty rows and columns in the analysis

>>> Sparsity.diag(3).is_orthonormal()
True
>>> Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 1], [0, 1]).is_orthonormal()

True
>>> Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 0], [0, 1]).is_orthonormal(True)

1
>> Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 0], [0, 1]).is_orthonormal(true)
0
>> [Sparsity.diag(2, 3).is_orthonormal(), Sparsity.diag(2, 3).is_orthonormal(true)]

◆ kron_contract()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::kron_contract ( const Sparsity &  sp_m,

static

Given an (mA*mB, nA*nB) pattern sp_m and an (xrow, xcol) pattern sp_x, computes the output sparsity. Both modes share the same (yrow, ycol) = sp_m.size() / sp_x.size() shape; what differs is which axis pair indexes the output:

  • inner = true: (i, j) ∈ y iff ∃ (r, s) ∈ sp_x with (i*xrow + r, j*xcol + s) ∈ sp_m; output indexed by the outer block of M.

  • inner = false: (r, s) ∈ y iff ∃ (i, j) ∈ sp_x with (i*yrow + r, j*ycol + s) ∈ sp_m; output indexed by the inner block of M.

◆ ldl()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::ldl ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  p,
bool  amd = true 
) const

Computes the pattern of the factor in A[p, p] = L*D*L^T, where L is unit lower triangular. Returns the pattern of the strictly upper triangular L^T (the unit diagonal is not stored) and the ordering p. A non-symmetric pattern raises an error. The numerical counterpart is ldl() applied to a matrix.

Parameters
amdIf true (default), a fill-reducing AMD ordering is computed and returned in p; if false, p is the identity
Returns
Pattern of L^T and the permutation vector p

>>> Lt, p = Sparsity.banded(4, 1).ldl(False)
>>> DM(Lt, 1), p
(DM(
[[00, 1, 00, 00],
 [00, 00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 00, 1],
 [00, 00, 00, 00]]), [0, 1, 2, 3])
>>> A = Sparsity.nonzeros(4, 4, [0, 3, 5, 10, 12, 15])
>>> Lt, p = A.ldl()
>>> Lt.nnz(), p
(1, [1, 2, 0, 3])
>>> try: Sparsity.upper(3).ldl()
... except Exception as e: print("not symmetric")
not symmetric


>> [Lt, p] = Sparsity.banded(4, 1).ldl(false);
>> DM(Lt, 1), p
[[00, 1, 00, 00],
 [00, 00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 00, 1],
 [00, 00, 00, 00]]
0 1 2 3
>> A = Sparsity.nonzeros(4, 4, [1, 4, 6, 11, 13, 16]);
>> [Lt, p] = A.ldl(); disp(Lt.nnz()), disp(p)
1
1 2 0 3
>> try, Sparsity.upper(3).ldl(); catch e, disp('not symmetric'); end
not symmetric


julia> ca.ldl(ca.Sparsity.banded(4, 1), false)
(4x4,3nz, [0, 1, 2, 3])
julia> A = ca.Sparsity.nonzeros(4, 4, [0, 3, 5, 10, 12, 15]);
julia> ca.nnz(first(ca.ldl(A)))
1
julia> try
           ca.ldl(ca.Sparsity.upper(3))
       catch e
           println("not symmetric")
       end
not symmetric

◆ permutation()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::permutation ( const std::vector< casadi_int > &  p,
bool  invert = false 
)
static

P is square with one nonzero per row and column, placed such that multiplying a column vector v from the left gives the same result as indexing it: P @ v == v[p]. The inverse of a permutation matrix is its transpose, so invert true returns the transpose pattern, for which P @ v puts v[i] at position p[i].

Parameters
pPermutation vector: every integer in [0, len(p)) exactly once; anything else raises an error
invertIf true, build the inverse (transposed) permutation

>>> P = Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1])
>>> DM(P, 1)
DM(
[[00, 00, 1],
 [1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00]])
>>> DM(P, 1) @ DM([10, 20, 30])
DM([30, 10, 20])
>>> DM(Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], True), 1) @ DM([10, 20, 30])
DM([20, 30, 10])
>>> Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], True) == P.T
True
>>> try: Sparsity.permutation([0, 0, 1])
... except Exception as e: print("not a permutation")
not a permutation


>> P = Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1]);
>> DM(P, 1)
[[00, 00, 1],
 [1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00]]
>> DM(P, 1) * DM([10; 20; 30])
[30, 10, 20]
>> DM(Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], true), 1) * DM([10; 20; 30])
[20, 30, 10]
>> Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], true) == P.T
1
>> try, Sparsity.permutation([0, 0, 1]); catch e, disp('not a permutation'); end
not a permutation


julia> P = ca.Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1]);
julia> ca.DM(P, 1)
DM(

 [00, 1, 00]])
julia> ca.DM(P, 1) * ca.DM([10, 20, 30])
DM([30, 10, 20])
julia> ca.DM(ca.Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], true), 1) * ca.DM([10, 20, 30])
DM([20, 30, 10])
julia> ca.is_equal(ca.Sparsity.permutation([2, 0, 1], true), ca.T(P))
true
julia> try
           ca.Sparsity.permutation([0, 0, 1])

◆ pmult()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::pmult ( const std::vector< casadi_int > &  p,
bool  permute_rows = true,
bool  permute_columns = true,
bool  invert_permutation = false 
) const

Nonzero (i, j) moves to (p[i], p[j]) when both rows and columns are permuted, to (p[i], j) for rows only and to (i, p[j]) for columns only. In matrix terms this is P^T*A*P, P^T*A or A*P with P the matrix of Sparsity.permutation(p). With invert_permutation the inverse of p is used instead, so that pmult(p, True, True, True) is the pattern of A[p, p].

Parameters
pPermutation vector; its length must equal the number of rows (if permute_rows) and the number of columns (if permute_columns)
permute_rowsPermute the rows
permute_columnsPermute the columns
invert_permutationUse the inverse permutation

>>> A = Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 1, 2, 0], [1, 2, 0, 0])
>>> DM(A, 1)
DM(
[[1, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 1],
 [1, 00, 00]])
>>> p = [2, 0, 1]
>>> DM(A.pmult(p), 1)
DM(

◆ qr_sparse()

void casadi::Sparsity::qr_sparse ( Sparsity &  V,
Sparsity &  R,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  prinv,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  pc,
bool  amd = true 
) const

Computes the patterns of V (the Householder vectors, a compact representation of Q) and R for the factorization of this pattern with its columns permuted by pc, plus the row permutation prinv used by the numerical factorization (qr_sparse on a matrix) and solution. V and R may have more rows than the pattern (the matrix is extended with zero rows when it has fewer rows than columns in the structural sense).

Parameters
amdIf true (default), the columns are reordered with the AMD ordering of A^T*A, returned in pc; if false, pc is the identity
Returns
V, R, prinv, pc

>>> V, R, prinv, pc = Sparsity.dense(3, 2).qr_sparse()
>>> V, R, prinv, pc
(Sparsity(3x2,5nz), Sparsity(3x2,3nz), [0, 1, 2], [0, 1])
>>> V, R, prinv, pc = Sparsity.banded(4, 1).qr_sparse(False)
>>> V, R, prinv, pc
(Sparsity(4x4,7nz), Sparsity(4x4,9nz), [0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 2, 3])


>> [V, R, prinv, pc] = Sparsity.dense(3, 2).qr_sparse();

>> V, R, prinv, pc
4x4,7nz
4x4,9nz

◆ scc()

casadi_int casadi::Sparsity::scc ( std::vector< casadi_int > &  index,
std::vector< casadi_int > &  offset 
) const

Node j is the j-th row/column and nonzero (i, j) is an edge from j to i. See Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems by Davis (2006).

Returns
The number of components n, the node indices grouped by component, and the offsets (length n+1): component i consists of the nodes index[offset[i]], ..., index[offset[i+1]-1], in increasing order.

The components are ordered so that the symmetric permutation A[index, index] is block upper triangular with n diagonal blocks; for a symmetric pattern it is block diagonal, with the block boundaries given by offset.

The implementation is a modified version of cs_scc in CSparse Copyright(c) Timothy A. Davis, 2006-2009 Licensed as a derivative work under the GNU LGPL

>>> A = Sparsity.nonzeros(4, 4, [0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15])
>>> DM(A, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00, 1],
 [1, 00, 1, 00],
 [00, 1, 00, 1]])
>>> n, index, offset = A.scc()
>>> n, index, offset
(3, [2, 0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 2, 4])
>>> DM(A, 1)[index, index]
DM(
[[1, 1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00, 00],
 [00, 00, 1, 1],
 [00, 00, 1, 1]])
>>> Sparsity.diag(3).scc(), Sparsity.dense(3, 3).scc(), Sparsity(0, 0).scc()
((3, [0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2, 3]), (1, [0, 1, 2], [0, 3]), (0, [], [0]))

◆ serialize() [1/3]

std::string casadi::Sparsity::serialize ( ) const

The string can be stored and turned back into an equal pattern with deserialize(). A null object serializes and deserializes as a null object. Pickling in Python uses this mechanism.

>>> s = Sparsity.diag(2, 3).serialize()

('str', True)

True

>>> pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(Sparsity.diag(2, 3)))
Sparsity(2x3,2nz)


>> s = Sparsity.diag(2, 3).serialize();
>> class(s), Sparsity.deserialize(s) == Sparsity.diag(2, 3)
char
1
>> Sparsity.deserialize(Sparsity().serialize()).is_null()
1

◆ sparsity_cast_mod()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::sparsity_cast_mod ( const Sparsity &  X,
const Sparsity &  Y 
) const

X and Y have the same number of nonzeros and sparsity_cast(X, Y) maps nonzero k of X to nonzero k of Y. Given that this pattern is a subset of X, the result is the subset of Y made of the nonzeros of Y whose counterpart in X is in this pattern.

>>> X = Sparsity.diag(4)
>>> Y = Sparsity.dense(2, 2)
>>> x = Sparsity.nonzeros(4, 4, [0, 10, 15])
>>> DM(x.sparsity_cast_mod(X, Y), 1)

 [00, 1]])

Algorithm 4.1 in Gebremedhin, Manne and Pothen, What Color Is Your Jacobian?, SIAM Rev. 47(4), 2006. Exploits symmetry so that fewer colors than uni_coloring are needed to recover all nonzeros of a Hessian. A non-symmetric pattern raises an error.

Parameters
ordering0 for the natural column order, 1 (default) to color in largest_first() order
cutoffIf more than this many colors are needed, a null Sparsity is returned

>>> H = Sparsity.banded(4, 1)
>>> DM(H.star_coloring(), 1)
DM(

 [1, 00, 00],
 [00, 1, 00],
 [00, 00, 1]])

True

5x1

The overload with invert_mapping additionally returns a mapping between the given entries and the nonzeros of the result (which are in column-major order). ◆ uni_coloring()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::uni_coloring ( const Sparsity &  AT = Sparsity(),
casadi_int  cutoff = std::numeric_limits<casadi_int>::max() 
) const

Greedy distance-2 coloring (Algorithm 3.1 in Gebremedhin, Manne and Pothen, What Color Is Your Jacobian?, SIAM Rev. 47(4), 2006): columns that have no row in common may share a color, so that one directional derivative per color recovers all nonzeros. This is the coloring used for forward-mode Jacobians (and, applied to the transpose, for reverse mode).

Parameters
ATThe transpose of this pattern, if already available; a null Sparsity (default) computes it
cutoffIf more than this many colors are needed, a null Sparsity is returned instead
Returns
A size2()-by-ncolors pattern: column c lists the columns of this pattern that received color c

>>> A = Sparsity.triplet(3, 4, [0, 1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3])
>>> DM(A, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00, 00, 1],
 [00, 1, 00, 00],
 [00, 00, 1, 00]])
>>> c = A.uni_coloring()
>>> DM(c, 1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [1, 00],
 [1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> c.size2(), [c.row()[c.colind()[j]:c.colind()[j + 1]] for j in range(c.size2())]
(2, [[0, 1, 2], [3]])
>>> A.uni_coloring(Sparsity(), 1).is_null()
True
>>> Sparsity.dense(3, 3).uni_coloring(), Sparsity.diag(3).uni_coloring()
(Sparsity(3x3,3nz), Sparsity(3x1))

◆ upper()

Sparsity casadi::Sparsity::upper ( casadi_int  n)
static

Column j contains the rows 0, ..., j, so the diagonal is included and the pattern has n*(n+1)/2 nonzeros.

Parameters
nSize of the square pattern, nonnegative

>>> DM(Sparsity.upper(3), 1)
DM(
[[1, 1, 1],
 [00, 1, 1],
 [00, 00, 1]])
>>> Sparsity.upper(3).nnz(), Sparsity.upper(3).is_triu()
(6, True)


>> DM(Sparsity.upper(3), 1)
[[1, 1, 1],
 [00, 1, 1],
 [00, 00, 1]]
>> Sparsity.upper(3).nnz(), Sparsity.upper(3).is_triu()
6
1
